item.title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems
item.abstract: Back to Articles Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems Published November 26, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 23 +17 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Kashif Rasul kashif Follow Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models. That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50. Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents? In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from. First, we'll start off with some context on swarms. The rise of the swarms We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem. But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so. A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment , coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same. Did cooperation help, or did we just spend more? Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries. Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided. This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute? We understand that question through this simple expectation. Figure 1. Sketch of the expectation we want to test: compare communicating and independent agents at matched budgets. We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily. Multi-agent Systems and Reinforcement Learning Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms. A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture. This creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training. A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward. Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are: A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog . A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL . Our first experiment: four agents ordering numbers We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows. Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is: #### [5, 5, 26, 78] The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list . One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates. This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful. The main communication tools are message(to, text) , read_messages() , and check_notifications() . A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone. We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy , with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments. Figure 2. The task and training loop.

item.title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
item.abstract: Back to Articles Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference Enterprise + Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 15 +9 Ryan Chesler emelryan Follow nvidia Marek Wawrzos mwawrzos Follow nvidia Steve Han steve-nvidia Follow nvidia We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. What Parse 3.5 produces Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training : Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry SFT teaches the capability; RLVR improves consistency We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents. We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) , using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) . Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content. A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output. Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods . The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer —and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35 . Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38 , including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts . Faster inference through architecture and DFlash2 A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs. Component Parse 2.0 Parse 3.5 Page preprocessing Fixed 2048 × 1664 canvas NaViT dynamic rectangular inputs Image-to-text connection Encoder–decoder cross-attention Compressed visual tokens as a causal prefix Decoder self-attention Multi-head attention GQA-8: 16 query heads, 8 key/value heads Speculative decoding One-token lookahead (MTP); optional DFlash2 NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory. The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead , and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens , or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token. Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details . In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively. Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it: Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts. Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output. Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests. In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements . Apply the same SFT/RLVR approach to your documents We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT , and NeMo RL GRPO , using vLLM to generate candidate answers. The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram : a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth. Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label . RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR. Figure 7.

item.title: Sakana AI Releases Namazu Small, a 30B Model Built on Nemotron 3 Nano
item.abstract: Sakana AI has announced Sakana Namazu Small , a 30-billion-parameter reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano. The Japan-based lab ran continued pretraining and post-training in-house, starting from Nemotron 3 Nano’s pretrained base. Sakana AI team states that the result beats NVIDIA’s 120B Nemotron 3 Super on its 25-benchmark average. Sakana Namazu Small is a 30B-A3B reasoning model from Sakana AI, tuned for web research and long-document QA. “Sakana Namazu” names models Sakana builds on open models and finishes with its own post-training. The larger Sakana Namazu is based on Kimi K2.6. Namazu Small is the compact member of that family. Sakana AI targets 3 kinds of work: everyday conversation, research with web search, and reading long documents. It was developed as a reasoning model. It organizes the information it needs and reasons step by step toward an answer. Sakana started from the pretrained base of Nemotron 3 Nano, not NVIDIA’s post-trained release. It then applied continued pretraining and post-training techniques built for this release. These sit on top of methods Sakana developed for the original Sakana Namazu. The base architecture matters for deployment. Nemotron 3 Nano is a hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model. NVIDIA lists it at 30B total and 3B active parameters , with context up to 1M tokens. Sakana compared it against 2 NVIDIA models, both post-trained by NVIDIA. These are Nemotron 3 Nano (30B-A3B) and Nemotron 3 Super (120B-A12B). The suite spans 25 benchmarks in 3 groups. All scores are self-reported by Sakana . Web research is the standout. On BrowseComp , Namazu Small scores 73.5 versus 36.1 for Super and 29.3 for Nano. On DeepSearchQA it reaches 84.3, against 65.4 for Super. Grounded long-document answering also jumps. LLM-jp LongBench rises to 86.0, versus 67.0 for the Nano baseline. FaithEval reaches 78.3 versus 59.1 for Super. LongBench-Cite hits 80.2 and ALCE reaches 60.2, both citation-focused tasks. Closed-book knowledge is the weak spot. On SimpleQA Verified it scores 6.8, below Super (18.1) and Nano (9.1). Japanese SimpleQA lands at 8.0, versus 24.9 for Super. HealthBench drops to 40.6, under Nano’s 47.5. Sakana itself says tasks using only internal knowledge did not improve much. Per benchmark, Namazu Small beats Super on 13 of 25 tests. It beats Nano on 22 of 25. Check out the official announcement , the Nemotron 3 Nano technical report and the Nemotron 3 Super model card . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . item.title: 頂尖商用級AI影片每秒只要5毛！中國開源新勢力拿下全球第一
item.abstract: 頂尖商用級AI影片每秒只要5毛！中國開源新勢力拿下全球第一 衡宇 2026-11-26 14:41:23 來源： 量子位 30秒一鏡到底，可自動編排鏡頭 衡宇 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 現在，花一杯奶茶錢，能生成什麼質量的AI影片？ 下面這條1080p的影片，生成價格是15元人民幣。 這是一條單次生成出來的30秒原片，不是後期剪輯的哦～ 在權威評測機構Artificial Analysis的圖生影片榜單裡， 生成這條影片的模型衝到了全球榜一。 妥妥躋身一線商用級標杆影片模型梯隊。 由衷感慨一下，影片模型這一波，國內玩家在全球賽場勢頭確實生猛！ 如你所見，它也made in China，系 影片初創公司Sand.ai剛釋出的480B影片模型MAGI-2。 MAGI-2擁有第一梯隊影片生成能力，每秒定價卻是同級別頭部閉源模型的十分之一。 全球AI影片創作平臺Higgsfield公佈了最新的影片生成模型效果與價格對比。結果顯示，MAGI-2顯著拓展了影片生成模型的帕累託前沿 （Pareto Frontier） ，在接近當前最強模型生成效果的情況下，重新定義了旗艦級影片生成模型的價效比。 價格大幅下探的同時，MAGI-2 在創作可控性上依然對齊商用生產標準。 該模型支援最高兩萬字元的複雜指令碼解析與毫秒級精準切鏡，能夠混合參考最多20份圖片、影片和音訊素材，並支援對已生成畫面的局部細節進行定向修改。 此外，MAGI-2在預訓練階段還 湧現出了對任務規則的理解以及自主推理與規劃能力。 你敢信這個影片模型居然會自己解數獨 （此處緩緩打出一個驚歎號） ？ Sand.ai表示，關閉提示詞增強 （PE） ，不給解題步驟，也不請語言模型當外援，MAGI-2僅憑任務指令和參考圖片，就在演示中完成了9×9數獨的求解。 這份自主規劃能力放到影片創作中，一段簡單的故事梗概，就足以讓MAGI-2自行編排分鏡、設計運鏡和人物動作。 釋出當日， Sand.ai宣佈計劃儘快開放MAGI-2模型權重 ，讓全球開發者有機會使用和進一步開發這一模型。 AI影片生成的開源陣營，這回有了衝擊全球頂尖水平的新籌碼。 從自主規劃到全模態局改的能力躍升 今年8月，Sand.ai推出了總參數114B的MAGI-2 Preview，本次新發布的MAGI-2總參數來到了480B。擴大模型規模後，團隊在預訓練評測中看到了意料之外的早期湧現現象。 前文提到的數獨求解便是其中之一。 給它一張9×9數獨參考圖，無需語言模型提前算出答案，也不用把解題步驟寫進提示詞，它自己就能看懂行列與九宮格約束，在影片裡一步步填入正確數字。 在影片創作的主戰場上， 這種能力展現為對敘事邏輯和鏡頭語言的自主理解能力。 即使創作者沒有交代全部細節，模型也開始嘗試自主補全情節、組織鏡頭。 下面這段魯肅與諸葛亮舟中對話的AI影片，創作者僅提供人物場景參考以及三處劇情節點，分別是“魯肅入舟落座”“二人交談”“孔明點破來意後魯肅神色一變”。 全程關閉提示詞增強 （PE） ，在完全不寫景別、機位和切鏡點的情況下，MAGI-2也自己琢磨出一套合理的構圖和視角切換，並把原本沒寫進指令碼的人物特寫和神情過渡補齊。 不過Sand.ai在模型技術報告裡沒有報喜不報憂，文中 分享了一個類似大語言模型“對齊稅”的觀察 —— 經過後訓練階段面向高審美偏好的微調後，成片電影感確實拉滿，但預訓練階段顯現的推理與泛化能力反而變得更難觸發了。 讓影片模型兼具審美與通用智慧，顯然還有不少研究空間。如何在高審美與強邏輯之間找到平衡，也將直接指導他們下一代訓練資料的設計方向。 回到MAGI-2的模型表現。 隨著畫質逐漸趨近實拍水準，AI影片模型的競爭已經進入更深層次的能力較量。 當前拉開影片模型差距的核心，已經卷到了複雜指令碼執行精度、鏡頭節奏把控以及長時敘事的連貫性等等。 MAGI-2能自己動腦子，但不代表它不聽指揮。 實則模型對於創作指令的執行精度相當出色。如果創作者想精確掌控每一個畫面節點，MAGI-2在指令遵循上表現得十分出色。 就拿切鏡來說～ 技術報告內公佈了一組時間軸控制測試。 在最考驗控制力的切鏡測試中，12次指定切鏡全部命中，平均時間偏差只有0.028秒，最大誤差不過0.08秒，也就是兩幀的差距，比行業主流模型普遍接近1秒的偏差精準得多。 技術報告還介紹， MAGI-2支援最長2萬字符的提示詞，創作者可以精細定義人物站位、動作序列、運鏡軌跡及事件發生時機。 精準控制鏡頭之外，MAGI-2還拓寬了影片創作的表達空間。 比如， 長鏡頭中的時空一致性 也是MAGI-2的能力亮點。 下面這段30秒的一鏡到底影片，帶著觀眾穿梭於梵高的《星月夜》、莫奈的《睡蓮》等五幅經典名畫之間。 五種藝術風格隨運鏡自然流轉，場景轉換、空間關係與鏡頭運動保持連貫。 單次30s成片是目前所有影片模型單次成片的最高時長，此外，單次生成即可覆蓋敘事的完整起承轉合，以及維持鏡頭運動與空間關係的連貫性，這些都是影片模型現階段的難點和攻克重點。 再看視覺維度，風格化是MAGI-2比較突出的一項能力。 它不僅支援寫實、繪畫、動畫和手工材質等多種畫風，還能直接從參考圖中提取配色與質感用於新內容生成。 在這條參考墨西哥鏤空剪紙的20秒手工定格動畫裡，無論是剪紙的材質、油畫的筆觸，還是二維動畫的運動特徵，MAGI-2都能在連續生成中較好地維持特定風格，避免畫風漂移。 此等豐富的視覺表達能力，還需要足夠靈活的創作手段來承載。 落到具體的工作流維度，全模態參考與精準局部編輯進一步降低了改片門檻。 MAGI-2單次最多支援20份媒體參考，包括10張圖片、5段影片和5段音訊。 人物外觀、場景佈局、藝術風格、動作及聲音，都可以通過不同素材加以控制。 比如這段《誤入巨花世界》，通過參考圖同時鎖定主角外觀、服裝及三個不同場景，藉助葉片與花瓣遮擋實現自然轉場。 參考圖鎖定： 最終成片： MAGI-2的一能力已經獲得了專業AI影片創作者的關注。 今年年初憑藉AI短片《牌子》出圈、獲得《流浪地球》導演郭帆公開稱讚的創作者DiDi_OK，在對MAGI-2進行初步測試後讚不絕口。 他評價道，能夠在單次生成中同時使用文本、影像、影片和音訊，為視覺敘事打開了新的想像空間，初步測試結果也頗為可期。 小tips，從演員、道具到聲音與語言，影片中的不同元素都可以成為獨立的編輯物件。 一段已經完成拍攝、運鏡和表演編排的影片，可以通過指令更換主角、植入新商品，也可以讓演員改說另一種語言，並同步重構口型。 生成完成的影片也可以成為可二次創作的內容資產。 對於品牌廣告、電商營銷、影視短劇等需要大量素材組合、多版本交付的場景，省下來的不只是明面上的生成費用。背後帶來的還有更大的創作空間，以及更低的內容迭代成本。 480B大塊頭如何跑出高性價比？ 今年8月釋出的研究版本MAGI-2 Preview，擁有114B總參數、約60億啟用參數。 短短幾個月後，正式版MAGI-2模型規模擴大至原來的4倍以上，達到480B總參數、約280億啟用參數。 規模擴展帶來的能力提升也相當顯著。在Artificial Analysis Video Arena v2.1上，MAGI-2四項任務的平均Elo評分從998.5躍升至1150.3，提升151.8分。 把模型做大四倍，同時把1080P成片定價壓在每秒0.5元，Sand.ai咋做到的？ 答案藏在Sand.ai從底層架構、訓練基建到資料管線的全鏈路效率設計裡。 模型架構層面，MAGI-2延續了Preview階段的兩項核心架構設計。 其一，單流統一Transformer （Single-Stream Unified Transformer） 。 文本、影片、音訊Token進入同一條序列，在統一的模型主幹中持續互動，為人物口型、動作擬音、環境聲場等音畫同步能力打下基礎。 其二，多頭潛空間混合專家架構 （Multi-Head Latent MoE） ，這也是MAGI-2能夠高效擴展至數千億參數規模的關鍵。 常規MoE採用先路由、後分發的機制，將完整Token動態傳送至不同裝置上的專家。隨著模型規模擴大，跨卡通訊、負載不均衡等問題容易成為訓練瓶頸。 出於硬體親和性與大規模分散式訓練效率等相關考慮，Sand.ai把每個token切分成多個獨立head，每個head自帶路由器和專家池。系統先按固定歸屬靜態分發切片，到了目標裝置本地再做動態路由和計算。 跨卡通訊量由此與啟用專家數量 （top-k） 解耦，通訊張量形狀可以提前確定，把“旱的旱死、澇的澇死”的負載傾斜、慢卡長尾和額外同步開銷壓了下去。 圍繞這套架構，Sand.ai自研了MagiFSDP、MagiMoE、MagiMuon等訓練基礎設施 ，分別最佳化參數分片管理、專家計算與通訊協同，以及分散式最佳化器效率。 在總FLOPs一致、各自採用最優配置的480B預訓練實驗中，Multi-Head Latent MoE相比LatentMoE實現了約22%的訓練加速。 架構與訓練系統解決了模型如何高效做大的問題，而如何將數千億參數的容量轉化為真正的智慧，則 對資料規模、資訊密度和處理效率提出了更高要求。 為了匹配480B的總參數體量，MAGI-2的預訓練資料規模較Preview擴大約3倍，達到4T Tokens。 依託自研資料管線，團隊僅用三週時間就完成了約10億條樣本的標註。 更有意思的是他們的資料篩選策略。技術報告 專門點出要“避免資料過濾陷阱 （Data Filtering Trap） ”。 它指的是影片模型訓練過程中容易過濾掉一些複雜的真實素材，以追求畫面美感。 為了讓模型充分學習真實世界的複雜性，Sand.ai團隊最後選擇保留多人互動、頻繁切鏡、螢幕文字、複雜聲場等資料。 技術報告顯示， 模型容量和資料規模帶來了明顯的規模紅利，像多餘手指、動作崩壞這些過去需要依賴後訓練修補的問題，在MAGI-2的預訓練階段就已大幅減少。 地基打得夠牢，後訓練就可以把精力全花在“精裝修”上。 這階段的強化學習 （RL） 重心從修補基礎結構缺陷，轉向打磨光影、紋理、毛髮、材質及聲學質感。 到了最後的 畫質輸出環節 ，MAGI-2用專用的潛空間時空超分模型把低清潛變數拉昇至1080P、25fps，並在超分階段重新注入原始參考圖。 因為基礎生成已經能錨定人物面部和文字的時空位置，超分模型重建高頻細節時就能直接對照原圖“抄作業”。 哪怕在長達30秒的複雜場景裡，遠景小臉的一致性和畫面文字清晰度也得到了明顯改善。 綜上，更大的模型容量、稀疏計算架構和系統最佳化，共同構成MAGI-2提升效能、控制計算開銷的技術基礎。 為全球影片開源生態抬高創新起點 技術報告末尾，Sand.ai坦陳了 當前MAGI-2模型的侷限性。 在極高速的劇烈運動中，MAGI-2生成的畫面的動作銜接與軌跡偶爾還會出現瑕疵，中、遠景二維動畫的局部動作有時略顯平滑，高度複雜聲場下的音效層次與物理質感也仍有提升空間。 此外，如何在後訓練階段兼顧成片審美與預訓練展現出的通用泛化能力，依然是團隊接下來要持續攻關的課題。 好訊息是接下來參與解題的隊伍有望進一步壯大。 Sand.ai宣佈，計劃儘快開放MAGI-2模型權重。 研究者可以在此基礎上探索影片模型的智慧邊界，開發者可以圍繞特定行業進行模型微調與應用開發，算力廠商也有機會推進不同硬體架構下的模型適配。 一個高水平基礎模型的開放，有望將原本集中於少數模型廠商的研發能力，轉化為更廣泛的生態創新能力。 向上探索影片模型的能力極限，向外釋放前沿技術的創新紅利—— Sand.ai正在把全球頂尖影片模型的能力上限，變成開源生態的創新下限。 item.title: Distilling Kimi-K3.1-Pro into Qwen3.8-27B: Teaching a model a new language
item.abstract: Summary The gap: Qwen3.8-27B answers in Thai when asked for Lao and scores 5.5 chrF++, while Kimi-K3.1-Pro scores 47.5 on the same test. The fix: We trained a LoRA adapter on about 3,800 of Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations using Together Post-Training. The result: The student writes Lao on every test sentence and scores 44.3, which is 93% of the teacher's score, and it keeps its Thai. The cost: All the experiments together cost \$260, and the code is in the post-training cookbook. While running some experiments we found out that Qwen3.8-27B , one of the most popular small language models (SLMs), can't write Lao, a Southwestern Tai language and the official language of Laos. If you ask it to translate an English sentence into Lao, it answers in Thai, Lao's closest relative, which uses an entirely different script. On the FLORES-200 Lao test set, the model scores 5.5 chrF++, a 0 to 100 score for how closely a translation matches a human reference, and only 11% of its outputs are in Lao script. Kimi-K3.1-Pro scores 47.5 on the same test. Admittedly, this is a niche use case, but the pattern is quite common: a small language model displays jagged intelligence, falling flat on a narrow task you care about while a larger, more expensive model handles it with ease. To fix this, we used Kimi-K3.1-Pro as a teacher and distilled its Lao translation ability into Qwen3.8-27B using Together Post-Training. After training on about 3,800 of Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations, the 27B student answers in Lao on every test sentence and scores 44.3, which is 93% of the teacher's score. It also kept its Thai translation ability, which interestingly turned out to be the hardest part. Our first attempt fixed Lao within 25 training steps but also lost Thai translating capabilities along with it. This post walks through how we found the gap and what ended up working. The code, settings and costs are in the second half. All the experiments together cost \$260. The student goes from writing Thai to writing Lao at 93% of the teacher's score, without losing its Thai capabilities. Finding the gap Kimi-K3.1-Pro beats Qwen3.8-27B on all 11 languages. Lao has by far the largest gap (49.0 vs 7.2). The metric we use is chrF++, which scores character and word overlap with a human reference translation, from 0 to 100. The important thing to know about Qwen's low Lao score is that, to chrF++, a Thai answer shares almost nothing with a Lao reference. When asked to translate into Lao, the student's output contained Thai script in 45 of 50 sentences and Lao in only 6: English: "We now have 4-month-old mice that are non-diabetic that used to be diabetic," he added. Qwen3.8-27B (base): “ปัจจุบันเรามีหนูอายุ 4 เดือนที่ไม่เป็นโรคเบาหวาน ซึ่งเคยเป็นโรคเบาหวานมาก่อน” เขากล่าวเสริม Kimi-K3.1-Pro: "ພວກເຮົາຕອນນີ້ມີໜູອາຍຸ 4 ເດືອນ ທີ່ບໍ່ເປັນໂຣກເບົາຫວານ ເຊິ່ງເຄີຍເປັນໂຣກເບົາຫວານມາກ່ອນ," ລາວກ່າວຕື່ມ. The base model's Thai is a reasonable translation, just in the wrong language. We'll come back to this in the results. One note on the numbers: on these 50 sentences Lao scores 7.2 for Qwen3.8-27B and 49.0 for Kimi-K3.1-Pro, and on the full 1,012-sentence test set it's 5.5 and 47.5. The test sets are listed under "How we built it." The plan: off-policy distillation Distillation trains a small model (the student) to behave like a large one (the teacher) on a given domain. There are two ways to do it. On-policy distillation (OPD) , described in Thinking Machines' post on the topic , has the student generate text and the teacher grade every token. It needs the teacher's log-probabilities on the student's tokens, which in practice means the two models have to share a tokenizer. Here since we are distilling Kimi into Qwen and they don’t share a tokenizer we went another direction. Off-policy distillation has the teacher generate the text and trains the student to imitate it with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In its simplest form it only needs the teacher's text. We used off-policy distillation. It keeps the teacher side fairly cheap: every teacher call is an ordinary serverless chat request, and Kimi-K3.1-Pro, which is quite a large model, never needs a training resource of its own. End-to-end pipeline: English sentences go to Kimi-K3.1-Pro, are filtered, and become SFT rows for a Qwen3.8-27B LoRA session on a Together Post-Training model resource. The steps: Collect English source sentences. Have Kimi-K3.1-Pro translate them, with thinking turned off. Drop any translation that isn't mostly in the target script. Fine-tune a LoRA adapter on Qwen3.8-27B with the translations as targets, evaluating on held-out test sentences as it trains. Save the adapter to the model registry. We trained the student on Together Post-Training. One model resource both trains the LoRA adapter and samples from it, so we could score the model as it trained. We scored every evaluation on four metrics: chrF++ against human references on FLORES-200 devtest: all 1,012 sentences at the start and end of each run, and 300 every 25 steps (every 50 or 100 in the two longest runs). Lao-script rate: the share of outputs whose letters are mostly Lao. This catches the Thai problem directly. Thai retention: chrF++ on 300 English-to-Thai test sentences, to check the model hasn't lost a language it already had. Round-trip adequacy: Kimi-K3.1-Pro translates each system's Lao back into English, and we score that against the original English. This checks meaning independently of reference style. Thai retention while also gaining Lao translation capability ended up being the trickiest part. The Thai surprise One run was a control: it trained on human Lao references, 945 of them from FLORES dev, with no teacher involved. Lao jumped from 6.7 to 43.3 within 25 steps. Then we looked at Thai. It had dropped from 46.7 to 11.7, and by the end of the run it was 5.3, with 0% of Thai outputs in Thai script. The model had learned to "write Lao when asked to translate", not "write the language you were asked for". The problem had swapped direction. English-to-Thai chrF++ on 300 test sentences. Training on human Lao alone collapses Thai; the mixed runs keep it. If we'd evaluated Lao alone, this run would have looked like the winner. It has the highest Lao score of any student in this post. Fixing Thai The Lao-only distillation run trains on Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations of the same sentences in place of the human ones. That slowed the damage a lot but didn't stop it. Thai held for two epochs, then slipped to 44.3 in the third, with 17 of 300 Thai answers written in Lao. Adding about 1,000 Kimi-K3.1-Pro Thai translations to the training data fixed it. Thai finished at 47.4 and 47.8 in the two mixed runs, above the base model, and never dropped below 47.3 at any evaluation. What each training mix does when you ask for Lao and when you ask for Thai. This is a great point to make about continual learning: when you teach a model something new, mix in data that protects what it already does well, so you don't get regressions in things you care about. Here that was Thai, the language most easily confused with Lao. Closing the rest of the Lao gap Thai was safe, but Lao was still short. With about 950 Lao examples each, the student trained on human references scored 44.7 and the two distilled students scored 41.8 and 41.9. Part of that is expected. Human references do better on a human-reference metric: FLORES dev and devtest were translated through the same human process, so training on dev teaches devtest's reference style. The distilled student learns the teacher's style instead. Scored against Kimi-K3.1-Pro's own translations, the distilled student climbed from 8 to 58 chrF++, and the student trained on human references reached 47. The other difference is supply. FLORES dev has 997 human references and no more, while Kimi-K3.1-Pro can translate any English text you have.

item.title: 任少卿帶著世界模型3.0來了！蔚來智駕訓練提效5倍，座艙也用上強化學習
item.abstract: 任少卿帶著世界模型3.0來了！蔚來智駕訓練提效5倍，座艙也用上強化學習 傑西卡 2026-11-26 11:23:35 來源： 量子位 李斌坦言：不做AI變革可能活不下去 傑西卡 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 蔚來把NOMI積累了9年的程式碼全刪了。 為了讓這個車載夥伴具備自主決策和行動的能力，蔚來徹底重構了其底層架構，引入超千億參數的大模型，打通整車數千項能力。 蔚來在自己12週年生日這天，舉辦了第三屆NIO IN蔚來創新科技日。李斌首先提出了他的兩個判斷： 智慧電動汽車是最具價值的Physical AI，汽車產業將是最大的AI應用產業。 在他看來，每一輛智慧電動汽車都具備感知、決策、執行的完整能力，而具身智慧機器人想要達到今天汽車產業的規模，還需要很長時間。 圍繞這一判斷，蔚來此次披露了產品技術和企業經營兩個層面的AI進展： 其一是 NOMI Intelligence 4.0 ，徹底重構底層架構，讓整輛車成為一個原生智慧體。 其二是 蔚來世界模型NWM 3.0 ，引入隱式世界模型，構建雙閉環強化學習體系，綜合訓練效率提升5倍，整車控制時延平均降低50%。 且今年8月對外宣佈了具身智慧創業訊息的 任少卿 ，此次依然擔綱蔚來智駕技術的釋出。 而在汽車之外，李斌還披露了一場持續三年多的內部變革——建設 AI原生組織（AI Native Organization） 。 目前，蔚來內部已開發數千個業務Agent，企業經營管理領域上線的各類應用超過7500個，研發綜合效率提升35%，庫存週轉速度提升23%。 僅在能源領域，通過AI精細化經營145萬塊電池，蔚來測算累計增加的電池全生命週期使用價值就超過了8億元。 在會後交流中，李斌坦言，推動這場變革背後有著非常現實的考慮： 我們不做這些事情，沒有出路，可能活不下去。 NOMI推倒重來，整輛車成為智慧體 大模型上車之後，智慧座艙其實還需要面對一個新的瓶頸： 模型理解使用者需求的能力的確越來越強，但 車輛執行任務的方式 卻逐漸跟不上了。 此前，NOMI採用的是 基於意圖分發 的技術架構。大模型負責理解使用者需求，再將指令分發至車控、導航、媒體等業務模組，沿著工程師預先設計的流程執行。 一旦需求涉及多個領域，或者使用者在任務執行過程中改變主意，工程師就需要編寫更多規則來銜接各個環節。 而且汽車的功能越豐富，系統的開發和維護成本就越高。 今年年初，蔚來決定徹底重構NOMI的底層架構，將主任務決策權交給大模型。 全新的NOMI Intelligence 4.0有兩項核心技術： NIM大模型矩陣，以及整車原生智慧體執行框架NOMI Intelligence Harness（NIH） 。 其中，作為智慧中樞的NIM情感智慧大模型，採用超千億參數規模的MoE混合專家架構，配合語音識別、全雙工互動、智慧決策、具身情感表達等專用模型，共同處理不同型別的任務。 在訓練方式上，蔚來將 閉環強化學習 引入智慧座艙，構建了使用者和車輛環境雙模擬模擬器。 一邊模擬使用者不同的表達方式及臨時改變的需求，一邊模擬車輛狀態和工具執行結果，讓模型在持續互動中學習如何完成任務。 基於百萬級訓練資料和超過60萬條評測資料，經過多輪迭代，NIM在典型車控任務中的完成率由40%多提升至95.3%。 不過，即便模型足夠聰明，也需要有調動整輛車能力的途徑。 蔚來在自研整車全域作業系統SkyOS·天樞的基礎上，構建了兩個核心中樞： Context Hub（全域情境感知中樞） ，匯聚整車近3000項原子級資訊，通過統一的語義表達，讓模型即時理解乘員、環境及車輛狀態。 Tool Hub（全域工具中樞） ，將整車22大領域、數千項車輛能力進行標準化，供模型自主檢索、呼叫和組合。 二者通過 Agent Loop（智慧體自主迴圈） 與大模型連線。模型圍繞使用者的目標選擇工具、執行任務，再根據車輛反饋的真實結果決定下一步行動。 舉個例子，使用者開啟空調卻感受不到出風，NOMI就可以自行排查各項設定。 假設問題出在前除霧模式上，NOMI就會徵得使用者同意，調整車輛狀態。整個過程無須工程師專門編寫完整的解決流程。 這種架構的價值在於，車輛每新增一項能力，都有機會參與更多此前未被定義的任務組合。 隨著模型自主決策的範圍擴大，蔚來也構建了 整車智慧體原生安全體系NAS ，將安全約束融入模型訓練及整車軟硬體系統。 互動方面，NOMI Intelligence 4.0實現了全雙工互動，可以邊聽、邊想、邊說，整體語音響應速度較上一代提升一倍以上，高頻車控操作可實現0.6秒響應。 NOMI的表情和動作，也由預設動畫轉向大模型生成。蔚來採集了大量真人交流時的神態、微表情和頭部運動資料，用類似訓練機器人的方式訓練NOMI。 按照計劃，NOMI Intelligence 4.0將於 今年12月 向首批使用者推送， 明年第二季度 進一步覆蓋其他智慧系統平臺。 對於車載AI而言，模型的智慧最終需要通過車輛的軟硬體系統轉化為實際行動。 而在智慧駕駛領域，這一過程還受到極為嚴苛的時間限制。 任少卿探索物理AI的Scaling新路徑 回想蔚來首次釋出世界模型，還是兩年前的創新科技日上，由任少卿推到臺前。 經過數輪迭代，世界模型與閉環強化學習逐漸成為蔚來智慧駕駛的核心技術路線。 隨著車隊規模擴大、模型能力提升，如何讓智慧駕駛沿著這條路線持續進化，也成了蔚來關注的核心問題。 在今年的創新科技日上，釋出 蔚來NWM 3.0 時，任少卿重點提到了 物理AI的Scaling路徑 。 除了擴大模型與資料規模，在他看來，物理AI還有一個重要的進化維度—— 執行效率 。 一輛以100km/h速度行駛的汽車，100毫秒就能駛出約2.8米。系統晚一點識別風險、作出決策，都可能影響最終的駕駛結果。 NWM 3.0引入了 時空聯合編碼技術 ，直接對連續畫面中的時空資訊進行建模，使模型能夠更加敏銳地捕捉其他交通參與者的運動趨勢，同時降低編碼環節的算力消耗。 演算法之外，蔚來還聯合 神璣晶片、AI工具鏈及底盤團隊 進行全鏈路最佳化，將智慧駕駛系統獲取的環境資訊與底盤控制深度結合。 最終，自研底盤控制時延降低78%，整車控制時延平均降低50%。 與此同時，蔚來還面臨著一個越來越突出的問題—— 資料增長的速度，遠遠超過了算力增長的速度 。 百萬輛級的車隊，每天能夠產生百萬小時以上的駕駛資料。 蔚來通過資料自進化體系，將 資料缺口發現、採集策略生成、資料探勘和收益驗證 等環節進一步自動化。 在相同人工投入下，資料探勘效率提升3倍，NWM 3.0的綜合資料量較上一版本提高7倍。 但 更多高價值資料也意味著更大的訓練開銷 ，尤其是引入世界模型之後，生成虛擬世界本身就需要消耗大量算力。 對於駕駛模型而言，這個虛擬世界其實未必需要以完整的影片畫面呈現。由此，NWM 3.0引入了 隱式世界模型 。 它省去了影片渲染環節，直接在神經網路的特徵空間中預測環境變化，讓駕駛模型在這一空間中完成閉環強化學習。 相比於每幀800萬畫素的影片畫面，隱式世界模型只需要輸出千量級的Token，相關訓練過程獲得百倍級加速。 原有的 顯式世界模型 也被保留下來，生成視角擴展至11個，承擔閉環測試與驗證任務。 通過顯式與隱式雙閉環強化學習體系，NWM 3.0在綜合資料量提高7倍的同時，綜合訓練效率提升5倍。 第三個技術方向，則是讓模型在複雜場景下更接近經驗豐富的駕駛員。 傳統強化學習依賴人工制定獎勵規則，但真實交通環境中，安全、效率、舒適性等目標並不總是一致，固定規則很難充分評價複雜的駕駛行為。 蔚來為此引入了 學習型獎勵模型（Reward Model） 。 它相當於駕駛模型的一位老師，能夠理解當前路況、預測不同行為可能產生的後果，並結合長期導航目標，對連續的駕駛決策進行綜合評價。 利用車隊積累的大量駕駛資料，獎勵模型學習區分不同駕駛行為的優劣，再指導駕駛模型的強化學習。據蔚來測試，NWM 3.0在複雜場景下的接管率降低40%。 按照計劃，NWM 3.0將在今年12月啟動備案，通過後面向四個智慧系統平臺推送。 此外，蔚來的智慧駕駛技術也進入了生產環節，目前每天有超過千輛新車在下線後自行駛向指定轉運地點。 從NOMI的架構重構，到世界模型訓練效率的提升，有限的資源條件始終是蔚來技術路線選擇的重要背景。 而如何提高資源的利用效率，也是一家汽車公司在經營層面需要解決的問題。 造車的公司，也要AI原生 李斌在現場舉了個很有意思的例子： 新疆賽里木湖的一座蔚來換電站， 周邊3公里內僅有7位使用者 ，預測日均換電量只有15單。單靠換電收入，這座站顯然無法達到立項門檻。 但按照蔚來新的投資決策體系，其 綜合投資回報測算值達到了2.3 ，值得建設。 這其中的差異在於，蔚來的智慧選址Agent還可以呼叫使用者需求預測、銷售助力及品牌價值模型，將換電站對長途出行、整車銷售和品牌影響力的貢獻納入投資決策。 原本分屬不同業務線、難以統一衡量的價值，由此有了共同的計算依據。 這背後涉及蔚來自2023年展開的一場組織變革—— AI Native CBU經營 。 李斌認為，全球汽車產業鏈總規模達到7萬億至9萬億美元，AI有機會為整個汽車產業帶來15%的效率提升，對應約1.2萬億美元的價值空間。 但即便AI能夠幫助工程師更快地寫完程式碼，一個研發專案是否值得投入、技術成果如何得到充分複用，依然是企業需要解決的問題。 局部提效與整體經營質量的改善之間，還隔著組織架構、業務流程和決策機制。 蔚來的選擇，是 將企業經營拆解為更小的單元 。一位使用者、一輛車、一塊電池、一座換電站，甚至一個研發專案，都可以成為 獨立的經營物件（CBU） 。 承擔經營責任的部門、團隊和個人，則需要明確圍繞這些物件投入了多少資源、創造了多少價值。 蔚來搭建了六層架構，將分散在各個業務系統中的資料，圍繞十幾類、上千萬個經營物件重新組織，再將各業務領域的知識和經驗沉澱為體系能力模型，供數千個業務Agent呼叫。 以能源業務為例，目前蔚來體系內管理著145萬多塊電池，資產原值超過1159億元。 每塊電池都有獨立的身份ID及完整的使用履歷，Agent可以持續監控電池健康狀態，並制定個性化延壽策略。 目前，相關策略累計執行超過7339萬次，測算增加的電池全生命週期使用價值達到8.14億元。 在充換電站的日常運營中，智慧充電Agent則可以根據電價、訂單預測及電池狀態進行分鐘級動態排程。兩年間，蔚來谷電利用率由30%提升至接近50%，額外消納谷電5.05億度。 類似的效率提升還發生在其他業務環節： 研發領域，超過1800個研發專案納入CBU經營體系，研發人效提升13%，綜合研發效率提升35%。 工業化領域，交付準時達成率達到99%，庫存週轉速度提升23%。 使用者服務領域，單Fellow（蔚來顧問）經營效率同比提升44.5%，價值創造同比提升8.1%。 …… 不過，業務效率的提升只是AI原生組織建設的一部分，更難改變的是企業原有的管理方式。 蔚來總裁秦力洪舉了一個例子： 有了Agent之後，Fellow可以根據使用者反饋自主制定工作計劃，那麼原本負責分配工作任務的門店總經理，其管理職責也需要重新定義。 企業的資源分配方式同樣需要調整。 目前，蔚來已經把 Token使用成本 也納入各部門的經營預算，研發團隊需要根據實際業務需求，權衡增加算力投入和增加人員投入各自能夠帶來的收益。 這些變化直接關係到企業內部的權責劃分、資源配置和績效考核，也意味著許多沿用多年的管理機制需要重新審視。 對於這場持續三年多的組織變革，秦力洪認為目前勉強做到了 60分 ，李斌卻只打了 二三十分 。 在李斌看來，技術架構決定組織架構，但技術可以推倒重來，長期積累的業務慣性和組織慣性卻很難在短時間內消除： 成為一家AI原生組織，甚至比開發一輛車更難。 智慧汽車的技術邊界正在被AI不斷拓寬，與之相伴的，是汽車企業研發方式、經營模式乃至組織形態的演變。 AI賦予汽車新的能力，也給百年汽車工業留下了新的命題。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 蔚來 傑西卡 item.title: Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon
item.abstract: Back to Articles Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon Team Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 19 +13 angt angt Follow ggml-org Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow ggml-org Abdennacer Badaoui badaoui Follow ggml-org The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance. Quick start You can choose Hardware , Model , and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201). In the Overview tab, compare quantizations for one hardware, model, and build. The two charts show PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens), both starting at context depth zero. In the Build history tab, track PP512 and TG128 across all recorded builds for the selected hardware, model, and quantization. In the Context scaling tab, see how token-generation throughput changes as the existing context grows, for the selected build, hardware, model, and quantization. What the numbers mean The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second: Test Workload What it helps you assess PP512 Process 512 input tokens How quickly the model processes a prompt TG128 Generate 128 tokens How quickly the model produces output Both tests start at context depth zero ( n_depth=0 ). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput ( avg_ts ). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows. How we run the benchmarks We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh , the build and installation project behind llama.app . The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration. The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M , Q8_0 , other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16 . Inspect and reuse the results The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model. Standard results use <build>/<hardware>/<model>/<quant>.jsonl . Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename. Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run. Join the conversation Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard , inspect the data , and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

item.title: AI 3D界的“X光”來了！一圖直出巴洛克雕塑，3D列印開箱即用
item.abstract: AI 3D界的“X光”來了！一圖直出巴洛克雕塑，3D列印開箱即用 衡宇 2026-11-26 20:39:08 來源： 量子位 還得是科班尖子生 衡宇 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 這段時間，大家拿GPT-6.2 Astra跑出來的3D效果真有點東西。 見過不少讓人眼前一亮的建模成果，這次我們想衝一把硬核難度。 看Astra能不能扛住考驗，完整復現這件結構繁複、細節密集的巴洛克雕塑。 3D模型剛一出來，我們都忍不住嘀咕。 這老Astra確實有點東西啊，挺牛！ 結果展開思考過程一看，好嘛，原來它自覺呼叫了VAST的開源模型TripoSR。 不允許呼叫別家模型的事發生！ 立刻命令GPT-6.2 Astra只准呼叫Blender，自己動手建模！ 結果是這樣的—— 雕塑表面磨了個皮， 人物、獅子和馬集體 走起了古意盎然的返樸路線。 有點淡淡的燒心。。。 難道這種地獄級雕塑已經超出當前AI 3D的能力上限了嗎？？？ 抱著試試看的心態，我們找VAST要到了Tripo最新3D模型，聽說更強—— 看效果，確實更強。 這位在“地獄級”群像雕塑裡穩住陣腳的專業選手，就是 VAST剛釋出的新一代高精度AI 3D基座模型Tripo H3.5 Preview。 相比上一代H3.1，H3.5 Preview在複雜結構還原、精細幾何生成、輸入輸出對齊，以及不可見部位的合理推斷等方面均有顯著提升。 目前，H3.5 Preview已上線Tripo Studio國際版。 （直通指路牌：https://studio.tripo3d.ai/） 在統一輸入、統一採用最高几何質量並剝離貼圖與法線貼圖的條件下 ，Tripo H3.5 Preview展現出了顯著優於其餘5款最新AI 3D旗艦模型的效能： 其中，在資深3D美術師對192組素模案例的盲評中，H3.5 Preview的生成結果拿下82次第一，佔比42.8%，勝率是第二名的2.3倍。 在實際生產環境中，專業3D美術師掌握著對“一件資產是否能進入管線”的判斷權，評測結果也 意味著H3.5 Preview的生成結果更符合實際生產標準。 △ 資深3D美術師對七款模型在192組並排案例中的排序分佈。“後兩名”指該組參評佇列中的最後兩位。模型D僅支援單檢視 （參評174組） ，各行第1名佔比按自身參評數計算。 為了衡量模型的多檢視三維重建能力——尤其是將不同角度的影像整合為統一、完整且無衝突的3D結構——VAST對比了幾個模型分別在單檢視和四檢視下的3D生成效果。 在覆蓋200餘個案例、結合Agent裁判與專家排序的盲測中，H3.5 Preview在22組彙總對照 （跨雙評測集與單/四檢視） 中無一敗績。 △ 雙裁判全量評測下，單檢視與四檢視案例上的Agent裁判得分對比，右側為差值。兩組案例對應不同資產，這裡比較的是兩類輸入模式下的整體表現，而非同一物體的前後變化。模型D僅支援單檢視。 此外， H3.5 Preview還有天花板級別的文字識別能力。 去除貼圖後，H3.5 Preview對3D浮雕文字的識別率高達90.7%，接近輸入影像的識別上限，顯著高於Tripo H3.1的46.1%。 △ 無貼圖網格經OCR引擎識別後，參考文本中每個字元的識別去向。幻覺字元指OCR讀出但原文中不存在的多餘字元。字元F1是衡量文字識別準確度的指標。 VAST介紹，這次技術升級的重點可以概括為兩個關鍵詞： 真實保真 （True Fidelity） ，細節有序 （Disciplined Detail） 。 來看Tripo H3.5 Preview的真功夫 為了摸清Tripo H3.5 Preview的真實底色，我們挑選了三類極易讓AI建模露餡的高難度場景，直接看它的無貼圖素模表現。 第一類，考驗浮雕還原能力。 作為輸入圖，這是一張紋理密度極高的青銅雙鳳三足鬲原畫。 青銅雙鳳三足鬲上，鳳凰的頸羽、翅羽與長尾覆蓋在細密的回紋底板上，外圍還環繞著珠點裝飾。 這道題的難點在於多個層級的紋飾密集分佈在同一曲面上， 模型既要識別不同紋飾的語義，又要準確表達它們之間的幾何高低關係。 放大H3.5 Preview的生成結果，雙鳳的頸羽、翅羽、長尾與底紋依然層次分明，器頸處的回紋帶也保持了較好的連續性。 這些細節本身就屬於模型的三維幾何結構，而不是依靠貼圖繪製出來的。 再來看看文字還原。 浮雕文字很考驗模型的細節還原能力：去掉貼圖後，文字必須靠表面真實的凸起或凹陷呈現，筆畫清楚、彼此分開，OCR才能讀出來。 相較於H3.1的變形，H3.5 Preview不僅精確還原箱子表面的文字，還保留了浮雕的深度。 第二類，考驗模型對複雜空間結構的理解和塑造。 細長結構坍塌、狹窄間隙粘連等問題，一直是AI 3D建模的重災區。 就拿遊戲美術場景中的典型硬表面資產科幻步槍來作例子吧！ 輸入圖中機匣與彈匣佈滿卷草十字徽記和骷髏裝飾，槍托更是將多層羽翼、圓形骷髏徽章、槽孔和鏈條紙帶塞進了極其狹小的區域。 即便如此，Tripo H3.5 Preview依然在保住機匣大面板結構的同時，讓骷髏保持了清晰的語義辨識度，卷草細枝也保留了獨立的分叉層次。 在另一輪實際測試中，我們選取了 渾天儀這一類對空間理解要求極高的複雜物件。 它由多層不同方向的環帶、支架、齒輪和球體巢狀而成，構件之間既相互交錯，又保持獨立；大量細長環帶在視覺上彼此遮擋，連線點、穿插關係和鏤空區域也很容易在生成過程中被誤判、粘連或填平。 模型不僅需要識別每個部件的形態，還要理解它們在三維空間中的層級、朝向與連線邏輯。 測試結果顯示，H3.5 Preview能夠較好地還原渾天儀複雜的空間結構：不同方向的環帶保持獨立，交錯構件之間的連線關係清晰，內部空腔與鏤空區域也得以保留。 也就是說，模型生成的並非一個“看起來像渾天儀”的整體輪廓，而是對其多層巢狀、彼此穿插的結構關係進行了更完整的幾何表達。 第三類難題，主要考驗模型對不可見部位的推演能力。 單圖生成3D有一個天然難題，那就是參考圖只能提供有限視角下的視覺資訊，物體背面、側面以及被遮擋的部分，都需要模型自行推斷。 以下方這張輸入圖為例，角色裝備與外形結構複雜。 想要讓生成的3D模型能夠自如地運用在遊戲資產創作中，盔甲從正面過渡至背部的結構、衣物褶皺依託軀體的延展形態，都需要由模型推斷並補全。 來看H3.5 Preview跑出來的結果： 再看H3.5 Preview生成的蠍尾獅 （波斯神話裡的經典幻想怪物） 的手辦，可觀察模型對遮擋區域的幾何推演與跨視角結構的連貫表現。 模型補全的背部結構與正面設計保持了較好的連貫性，不同視角下的形體和部件關係也基本一致。 對比輸入圖來看，成果實屬不賴： 更重要的是，這種高精度表現不是靠反覆抽卡碰運氣換來的。 通過擴大模型容量與系統化訓練，Tripo H3.5 Preview大幅提升了首輪生成的可靠性，即使面對複雜、多樣的真實使用者輸入，也能顯著減少結構錯誤，讓單次生成的結果更加穩定、可用。 打破盲目堆高面數和解析度後的“虛假保真” 近一年來，AI 3D賽道湧現出一批以“高面數”“高體素解析度”為主要賣點的模型。 然而，在實際生產環節中，參數規模並不等同於幾何質量—— 將模型匯入切片軟體進行3D列印，或匯入DCC工具進行烘焙後，常會暴露出非流形幾何、自相交、局部破損，以及細節粘連、結構關係失真等問題，難以滿足後續製作流程對模型完整性與可編輯性的要求。 過往的不少AI 3D模型演示效果亮眼，落地實操時卻問題頻發，根源就在於這套容易想當然的評價邏輯。 其間有幾個看似理所當然，實則錯誤的評價標準。 其一，高面數、高解析度≠高質量還原。 歸根結底，取樣解析度和麵數只是細節得以呈現的載體，並不等同於細節本身。 如果模型對三維結構的理解和幾何表徵能力沒有同步增強，一味提高體素網格解析度，或將三角面數堆至千萬級，就像用更高畫素翻拍一張失焦的照片：取樣更密，不代表輪廓和結構更清晰。 這樣的參數提升不會自動生成準確的結構，反而可能將生成過程中的不確定性與偽影一併放大——表面噪點增多，硬表面折邊模糊，窄縫與交疊處粘連。 無論是3D列印還是遊戲資產製作， 冗餘的幾何噪點同樣消耗面數，錯誤結構也能被高解析度網格完整呈現。 其二，紋理細節≠幾何細節。 雕刻、浮雕、文字、Logo、齒輪和倒角等精細特徵，如果僅僅依靠貼圖“畫”在表面，模型本身並沒有對應的立體結構。 其三，渲染效果好、輪廓對齊≠結構完整、生產可用。 精美的渲染圖可能掩蓋了薄結構坍塌、鏤空粘連、交叉姿態變形以及背面結構錯誤等問題。 真實操作流程中，3D列印通常要求模型具備閉合、無非流形問題的網格結構，數字資產生產則對拓撲質量、結構完整性與可編輯性有著各自的要求。任何幾何缺陷都可能轉化為額外的人工修復成本。 隨著AI 3D逐漸走進專業生產流程， 這種依靠參數堆砌和貼圖修飾營造的“虛假保真”必須被打破 ，幾何細節的準確性、合理性與可用性，也需要被放到更重要的位置。 如何讓每一份幾何表達預算都花得有價值？如何做到該精雕細琢的地方毫不含糊，該平滑的地方又不畫蛇添足？ 這就要展開說說Tripo H3.5 Preview此次技術升級所圍繞的兩個關鍵詞，“真實保真 （True fidelity） ”和“細節有序 （Disciplined details） ”。 所謂真實保真 ，核心在於忠於參考圖、忠於幾何、忠於生產。 它不僅要求準確還原整體比例、部件結構與未見側面的合理形態，更強調將細節實打實雕刻進三維幾何，確保網格乾淨閉合，直接解決生成結果是否準確、真實、可用的根本問題。 比如以下這組測試中，H3.5 Preview既還原了盔面的鍛造痕跡，也保留了盔甲的結構——從底部開口能看到內壁。 相較之下，模型E對盔面材質、毛髮細節的還原度不足，且內腔沒有打通。 另一組用網球拍所做的測試中，H3.5 Preview準確還原了網線的縱橫交織，但模型E生成的拍面卻連成一片。 △ 左側，Tripo H3.5 Preview的縱橫拍線之間留有網孔，可以直接看到背景；右側，模型E雖然有網格狀紋路，拍面卻連成了一片。 這說明Tripo H3.5 Preview能夠在整體排布、局部形態與細微刻線之間保持一致，讓細節既豐富，又有清晰的結構與含義。 所謂細節有序 ，則聚焦於局部細節的語義準確性、結構合理性與表面乾淨程度。 模型會在面部特徵、手指、扣件、齒輪、通風口、清晰可讀的文字和銳利倒角等關鍵部位精準建模，同時克制地讓相鄰的平滑表面保持平整無噪點，從而真正解決幾何細節的質量問題。 在實際測試中可見，H3.5 Preview既能精準還原人物面部，也能保持盔甲上龍頭浮雕、背景祥雲紋飾之間的層次感。 幾何精度越高，越需要模型準確把握物件的整體形態與結構關係。 比如，豐富的細節、乾淨的表面，兩者向來難以得兼：缺少細節、光潔的團塊 （模型A） ，容易在整潔度上拿高分；充滿噪點、過度銳化的表面 （模型B） 又能營造出高細節的“幻覺”。 評測顯示，在單檢視和四檢視生成結果下，Tripo H3.5 Preview在保持一定表面整潔度的同時，擁有絕對領先的細節還原能力。 值得強調的是，在這兩個維度上，它的能力甚至都超過了支援面數更高的模型 。 △ 各模型在Agent裁判“幾何細節”與“表面整潔度”兩類檢查項上的通過率，氣泡麵積代表單網格三角面數中位數。折線連線在雙軸上不被任何其他模型同時超越的Pareto Frontier模型 （指在多個指標之間達到最佳平衡、任何一項提升都必然犧牲另一項的最優解集合） 。 這依賴於Tripo經過持續迭代和落地所建立的技術判斷力：哪些能力真正提升了模型的還原度，哪些只是增加表面細節、放大幾何噪聲。 基於這些判斷，Tripo不斷調整技術路徑，在細節豐富度與結構準確性之間取得更好的平衡。 真正跑通3D列印與生產管線 當精細結構能夠被真實地生成出來，AI 3D的能力就有了新的檢驗方式。 把模型交給3D印表機。 從科幻角色的護甲接縫與裝備扣件，到東方武將的獅首肩甲與層疊浮雕，再到龍首的鱗片、角冠與皮膚褶皺，這些案例都要求模型將複雜細節轉化為清晰、完整的實體幾何。 Tripo H3.5 Preview生成的模型可直接進入切片、支撐設定等列印準備流程，並在列印實物中保留鮮明的輪廓與豐富的層次，讓螢幕上的結構與細節真正落到實體之上。 以往AI生成的模型往往還需要人工修復幾何缺陷，才能滿足列印要求。 此次升級中，Tripo H3.5 Preview重點瞄準的應用方向就是 對幾何質量要求極高的工業級高精度3D列印。 Tripo H3.5 Preview能夠直接生成表面完整閉合的3D網格 （即原生水密體） ，減少後續人工修模的工作量，為模型進入3D列印流程提供基礎。 伴隨H3.5 Preview釋出，Tripo同步上線了 可列印檢測與自動修復 兩項功能。 前者能夠根據目標列印尺寸，自動檢測模型的薄壁 （thin walls） 、水密性 （watertight） 與非流形邊 （non-manifold edges） ；後者則支援一鍵修復孔洞和非流形邊，並根據列印工藝及尺寸要求調整壁厚。 整個過程在同一介面內完成 ，省去了使用者在建模軟體與切片工具之間來回切換、手動修模的部分工作，讓AI生成的3D模型更順暢地進入實體列印環節。 △ 對三方資產的可列印性檢測。 模型生成後，無需繁瑣的人工修復就能進入切片與實體列印流程，適配桌面FDM、光固化與全彩裝置。 事實上， Tripo在3D列印產業鏈上已經有了不少合作夥伴。 它是最早接入拓竹MakerWorld的AI 3D大模型；今年7月，Tripo又與黑格科技達成戰略合作，將全彩內容生成引擎接入HeyVerse平臺。 如今，包括拓竹、黑格、創想三維、縱維立方、愛樂酷在內的頭部硬體廠商均已接入，Tripo系列模型提供的AI建模能力正在融入主流3D列印裝置的內容生產生態。 BTW，除了實體列印， Tripo H3.5 Preview在遊戲等數字內容生產場景中，同樣有不容小覷的價值。 在傳統的3A級遊戲資產製作中，高模往往需要經歷基礎形體搭建、反覆對照參考調整比例、細節雕刻等多輪打磨。複雜角色的面部、護甲與裝飾尤其依賴美術師逐層塑造，製作週期長，人力投入高，也容易在反覆修改中推高成本。 對於這類追求高保真細節的資產，Tripo H3.5 Preview能夠提供結構與細節較為完整的初始高模，前置完成部分耗時的參考對齊與形體補全工作，讓美術師將更多精力投入後續編輯、設計調整與細節精修，加速資產製作流程。 在更追求迭代效率與引擎直出的遊戲管線中，VAST則佈局了主打原生四邊面拓撲的Tripo P2.0。 item.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
item.abstract: Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue , the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation . By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings. The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows. Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion → For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks. Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion → Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market. Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company. The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion → Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work. Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows. Jump to the infrastructure discussion → Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected. The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there. Jump to the agent platform discussion → Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did. When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today. Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion → What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand. Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over.

item.title: Rethinking read replicas for the lakebase architecture
item.abstract: The idea behind read replicas makes sense: when your app gets busy, you add a couple of read-only replicas, route the heavy reads to them, and let the primary focus on writes. In practice, that rarely works well. In traditional managed Postgres, a replica is a physical clone of the primary: its own instance, its own storage volume, and its own copy of every page. That makes replicas impractical for scaling reads on the go. They take minutes to hours to create, each one adds a full copy of the data to your bill, and they keep running long after the traffic spike is gone. What was supposed to be a nimble way to scale reads turns into one more instance to manage. Like other DX problems with OLTP databases ,this is an architecture problem that comes from running things as a monolith. In Lakebase Postgres, a read replica doesn't copy anything - it's one more compute attached to the storage the primary already uses. It's ready in seconds, adds no storage, and scales to zero when nobody is reading from it. Replicas in Postgres are asked to do two jobs: standbys for high availability, and read replicas for scaling reads. This post is about the second one. (High availability replicas are also fascinating, and we'll cover how we approach HA in the lakebase architecture in a future post.) Picture a typical Postgres deployment on a managed service like Amazon RDS. Postgres runs on a single instance, with its data on a storage volume attached to that instance. Backups and snapshots go to S3. Every query the app sends, reads and writes, lands on that one machine. Traffic keeps growing. Most of it is reads, and at some point the instance runs out of CPU and memory to serve them. On a monolithic service like RDS, you have two ways to scale: move to a bigger instance, or add a read replica and send some of the reads there. On RDS, adding a read replica pretty much means building a second machine: The work scales with the database. A bigger database means a bigger snapshot and a bigger volume to fill. A busier one means more WAL to replay before the replica catches up. On a small database, that can take minutes. On a large one, it can take hours. And "available" doesn't mean done. On RDS, the new replica's volume keeps loading data blocks from S3 in the background after the replica comes online, and AWS notes that performance might not be at its fullest until that finishes . The process isn't free for the primary either: creating the snapshot briefly pauses its I/O unless it runs Multi-AZ, and a long-running transaction on it slows the whole thing down. Put all of that together, and you get a set of problems that share one root cause: in a monolith, the replica is a physical clone of the machine. The result is the opposite of what replicas promised. Instead of an elastic way to scale reads, you get one more static, overprovisioned piece of infrastructure to maintain. So many teams do the rational thing: they oversize the primary for the peak and skip replicas altogether, or they keep one replica running full time, just in case. The principle behind read replicas is sound. It's the monolithic implementation that broke them in practice. The lakebase architecture sets the stage for building replicas differently, making them much more usable: Services like RDS run Postgres as a monolith: a single machine that owns both execution and durable state. Lakebase Postgres splits those responsibilities apart : The four problems of traditional replicas come down to two: Separating compute from storage fixes both. Since compute owns nothing durable, nothing stops more than one compute from attaching to the same storage. That is the whole trick behind replicas in the lakebase. A read replica in Lakebase Postgres is an independent, read-only compute that reads from the same storage as the primary. Creating one looks like this: That is it. Nothing in that list depends on the size of the database, which is why creating a replica takes seconds on a small database and on a large one alike. It also adds no replication work to the primary: the primary keeps streaming WAL to the safekeepers as usual, and the replica reads from the safekeepers, not from the primary. In a traditional setup, N replicas means N + 1 copies of the database: one on the primary's volume and one on each replica's volume, each provisioned, filled, and billed separately. In Lakebase Postgres, N replicas still means one copy. The data lives once in the storage layer, and every compute on the branch, the primary and all of its replicas, reads from it. A replica does keep a local cache, in shared buffers and on its local NVMe, but a cache is not a copy. It starts empty, fills from the pageserver with the pages the replica actually uses, and holds nothing durable. For deploying and running replicas, that means: Since a replica is just a compute, it gets everything a Lakebase compute gets, configured independently of the primary: Being lighter to deploy is half of the story. The other half is that Lakebase replicas cost much less to run, for two reasons: A traditional replica is an instance, and an instance bills by the hour, whether it serves one query or a million. You size it for the peak, and you pay for the peak around the clock. A Lakebase replica bills for the compute it actually uses: On RDS, every replica comes with its own storage volume, sized for the full dataset and billed like the primary's. Three replicas on a 1 TB database means paying for 4 TB of storage. In Lakebase Postgres, the same setup still means paying for 1 TB. Storage is billed for the data in the storage layer, and replicas add nothing to it . Replicas add compute, never storage. Put together, the cost of a replica follows the reads it serves, not the size of the database or the number of hours in a day. That is what turns a replica from something you budget for in advance into something you can create for a single job and delete afterwards. When a replica is ready in seconds, adds no storage, and costs nothing while it's idle, patterns that never made sense with traditional replicas start to make sense. You can create one replica per workload instead of sharing one replica across everything. When you're done, you can delete it, or let it scale to zero. Just a few examples on how Lakebase customers use them: If your app is heavy on reads, or you want the primary to spend its resources on writes, you can send reads like feeds, product pages and search to one or more replicas. Writes, and any read that needs to see a write it just made, stay on the primary. Every time there’s a launch or you’re experiencing a traffic spike, you can immediately add a read replica and let it scale to zero as traffic settles. You can also give dashboards, BI tools, and reports their own compute, so heavy scans don't compete with your app for CPU and cache. the primary, like how many orders are stuck in pending right now or which customers hit a checkout error in the last hour. You can of course set up read-only roles in Postgres, but when an agent, a partner, an auditor, or a third-party tool needs to look at live data, it's often quicker to give them a read replica. They get current data, and there's no way for them to change it. Plenty of background work mostly reads - nightly CSV exports, a search index rebuild, a newsletter going out to your whole list. When you run them on the primary, these jobs compete with your users for CPU and cache, and the app slows down whenever they kick in. If you point them at a replica instead, your users will never notice (and you’ll gain peace of mind). The idea behind read replicas was always right. They keep heavy, non-critical read jobs from slowing down production, and they're a way to add compute capacity temporarily. But when Postgres ran as a monolith, that was hard to do in practice: every replica was an expensive physical clone with its own upkeep.

item.title: Top 5 Open-Source Alternatives to OpenAI Dots
item.abstract: Top 5 Open-Source Alternatives to OpenAI Dots Explore top open-source alternatives to OpenAI Dots for building always-on AI agents with persistent memory, task automation, custom skills, and local deployment. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 26, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence What if you had an AI assistant that worked for you 24/7, even when you're sleeping or away from your computer? That's the idea behind OpenAI Dots , an always-on AI agent that brings the personal assistant experience popularized by projects like OpenClaw into ChatGPT . You can interact with it from your phone, give it instructions, schedule tasks, connect your favorite apps, and let it work in the background. It can research topics, manage emails, monitor projects, build websites and applications, and even use coding tools and reusable skills to complete more complicated tasks. Unlike a regular chatbot, Dots has its own cloud computer, remembers your ongoing projects, and can continue working without constant instructions . It can also ask for your approval when important decisions need to be made. But what if you want the same experience without depending entirely on OpenAI? What if you want to run your own agent, choose your AI models, install custom skills, and have more control over your data? In this article, we will explore five open-source alternatives to OpenAI Dots that offer persistent memory, automation, messaging integrations, and tools for building your own always-on AI assistant. 1. OpenClaw OpenClaw is probably the closest open-source alternative to OpenAI Dots. It's a personal AI assistant that runs on your computer or server and connects to messaging platforms like WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, and more. What makes OpenClaw interesting is that it doesn't just wait for your next message. You can configure scheduled tasks and heartbeat checks so it can monitor ongoing work, send updates, and remind you about important things. It also supports persistent memory, browser automation, custom skills, and different AI models. You get a web-based Control UI to manage your assistant, conversations, and settings. The biggest drawback is setup and maintenance. Since you're running it yourself, you need to configure its tools, security, and model access. 2. Hermes Agent Developed by Nous Research , Hermes Agent takes a slightly different approach to personal AI assistants. Instead of only remembering conversations, it focuses on learning from experience. For example, when Hermes completes a task, it can turn useful knowledge into reusable skills. Over time, it can improve those skills, search previous conversations, and remember information about your preferences and ongoing projects. It also supports scheduled jobs, subagents, messaging integrations, and different language models. Another useful feature is Hermes Desktop, which provides a proper interface for chatting, managing skills, viewing tool activity, and working with files. A browser dashboard is also available. It's particularly interesting if you want an assistant that becomes more useful as you continue working with it. 3. QwenPaw QwenPaw , previously known as CoPaw, is an open-source personal assistant built around persistent memory, automation, and agent collaboration. One of its interesting features is its three-layer memory system. It maintains working context, conversation history, and a personal knowledge base that can evolve over time. You can also create multiple agents with their own memories and skills and have them collaborate on more complicated tasks. QwenPaw supports scheduled execution, messaging platforms, browser tools, and document processing. It comes with a web console and a desktop application, although the desktop version is still in beta. You can use commercial AI APIs or run supported models locally, giving you more control over cost and privacy. 4. OpenHuman OpenHuman is another interesting alternative, especially if you want an AI assistant that works directly on your computer. It's built using Rust and takes a local-first approach to memory, agent execution, and automation. You can use its desktop application to interact with agents, manage workflows, and work with files and applications. It supports browser and computer automation, persistent memory, scheduled workflows, and approval steps for actions that need your permission. What makes it different is its focus on efficiency and running multiple agents with relatively low infrastructure overhead. However, OpenHuman is still in early beta, so you should expect some rough edges. 5. nanobot If you're looking for something lightweight, nanobot is worth exploring. It's a Python-based personal AI agent that can run locally or on your own server. Despite its relatively small architecture, it supports persistent memory, scheduled automations, web tools, file operations, and integrations with messaging platforms. It also comes with a browser-based interface where you can manage conversations, view tool executions, configure models, and monitor automation tasks. Another advantage is its flexibility. You can connect commercial AI providers or use locally hosted models through tools like Ollama . For developers who want to understand, customize, and extend their personal AI assistant, nanobot provides a practical starting point. This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. # 26th November 2026 , 6:08 am / backups , sqlite GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery . Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. # 24th November 2026 , 4:53 pm / history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer . GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. By my rough estimate that is what it would cost in compute to clean up everyone's data for them, properly and automatically. I cannot do it for everyone. I am fed up with what everyone is put through. So here is my response: f*ck_data_brokers.py One Python file. No dependencies. Free. It runs on your computer, keeps your details on your computer, and makes data brokers delete you. Star this repository Every star is one more person these companies have to answer. The more stars, the sooner they learn their lesson. It costs you one click. It costs them a compliance department. The platinum option: let Agent Garrett do it This tool is free and always will be. It is also work: 600 companies, their excuses, their forms, their silence, and then next month they collect you again. Agent Garrett is the service I built to do all of it for you. Set it and forget it(you can do it for free with this tool if you cannot afford the subscription!). Persistence is guaranteed. Agent Garrett does not get bored, does not get tired and does not take "use our form" for an answer. A broker can stall a person. It cannot outlast a machine that never stops asking, and that is how removal happens: not with one letter, but with the one that never stops coming. Who these people are Data brokers are companies you have never heard of. They collect your name, your address, your phone number, your relatives and your habits, without asking. They sell all of it to anyone with a credit card. Then they write "we value your privacy" at the bottom of the page and expect you to keep a straight face. More than 600 of them signed a government registry admitting, in writing, that selling people is their business. That makes them very easy to find. What this does to them Gets the list of registered data brokers. All 600 and more. Writes each one a real legal deletion and opt-out letter in your name, quoting the law where you live. Sends the letters from your own free mailbox, or hands them to you ready to send. Reads what they write back and tells you which excuse it is and what to answer. Chases the ones that go quiet and tells you where to file a complaint about the ones that refuse. The tool is rude about data brokers. The letters are not. They are firm, correct and legal, because the goal is to leave a broker with nothing to hide behind. What you need Python 3.8 or newer. Check with python --version . If you do not have it, get it free from python.org . An email address. A free one is fine. That is all. No account, no subscription, no AI required. Use it without AI Download fuck_data_brokers.py , open a terminal in that folder, and run: python fuck_data_brokers.py You get a menu. Go down the list: Tell it who you are. Name, email, city, and where you live. No street address, no birthday, no ID. Brokers get the minimum. Get the list of data brokers. Write the deletion letters. It writes 20 at a time. Send them. Sending the letters, for free You do not need to pay for an email service. Pick whichever is easier. The send page (no setup at all). If the button does not open your email, the page also has copy buttons for the address, the subject and the letter. When you are done, run python fuck_data_brokers.py sent all so the clock starts. Let the tool send them. Run python fuck_data_brokers.py send . It sends through your own mailbox and knows the settings for Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and iCloud. It asks for an app password , which you create in your email account's security settings after turning on two-step sign-in. The password is used once and never saved. A separate free address just for this is a good idea. Their replies stay out of your real inbox. Put it on a schedule One command does everything that needs no decision from you: python fuck_data_brokers.py auto It refreshes the broker list, writes the next 20 letters, writes reminders for brokers that are late, and rebuilds your send page. Run it as often as you like; it never writes to the same broker twice. Add --send and it also sends, using the app password in the FDB_SMTP_PASS environment variable. Run it once a week and the whole list is covered in a few months without you thinking about it. On Linux or macOS, add a line to your crontab. On Windows, create a weekly task in Task Scheduler that runs the same command. 0 9 * * 1 python3 /path/to/fuck_data_brokers.py auto The one thing it cannot do for you is read your inbox. When a broker answers, paste the reply into reply . When a broker says "use our form" Some will not act on an email.
