item.title: AI #196: The Return
item.abstract: It is traditional on Thanksgiving for my weekly update to give thanks. This year, more than ever, I am thankful for all those who are increasingly rallying to fight the good fight and give us a chance to make it out of all this alive and well. Increasingly, I am thankful that we are not dead yet, nor do we yet seem doomed. I am thankful to all my readers. I can tell that you are listening, and taking what I say to heart, and I truly appreciate it. I am thankful that I am trusted to curate and bring this information to you, that many are listening to my takes and advice in both public and private, and that I have become trusted to distribute remarkably large amounts of money to causes that I believe in. I am thankful to my wife and wonderful family. Whatever else is going on in the world, I know I can count on them. I don’t know that I could do this without that. Most saliently right now, however, I am immensely thankful that I finally did get to take a real vacation, with wonderful friends both old and new. Then I came back. Will I ever dare take a vacation again ? There really is a lot going on right now. While I was gone, the market dropped so much that President Trump intervened to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . Oh, and also Claude and Levent Alpoge proved the Riemann Hypothesis . Anthropic has now used Claude to cut the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis down from 17.4 million lines of Lean to 76,000, a drop of 99.6%. The proofs have continued to come fast and furious, with Google getting in on the act as well. Scott Aaronson shares his thoughts on the extended Mathocalypse, which are summarized by, and I quote, ‘HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT.’ It feels like so long ago already, but I continue to recommend Dwarkesh Patel’s interview with Paul Christiano , which I covered in full on Friday . Christano’s Hinton lectures ( day 1 , day 2 , day 3 ) also remain excellent. OpenAI shared how the perplexity of their pretraining has improved over time , called upon others to do the same and proposed using this as a pacing measure. I will be covering that tomorrow. There has been more recent discussion about Handoverism. If we build superintelligence or otherwise very powerful AIs, how will we avoid handing over power to them? If we cannot avoid this without doing something even worse, perhaps we should not build those AIs in the first place. Many take shots at Anthropic, claiming that their plan is Handoverism, whereas I assert that The Plan is No Plan. In the face of the latest accusations, Dario Amodei replied at length on Twitter . I will be covering these events and debates in the coming week. That still leaves an unusually large weekly post. Lost in all this was the release by OpenAI of Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2. I covered their model card , but have not offered the capabilities post. I hope to do that this week. I also haven’t covered Gemini Neon at the level it likely deserves, given that feedback has been remarkably positive. Eli Tyre has Fable estimate that the software he has built over the last two months, using only a Claude subscription and 70 hours of direct screen time, would have previously taken at least 7k hours and $500k. Use LLMs to create a Calculator Double Crux to settle your disagreements, as in having the AI create a model that both of you can play around with. Colgate replaces its market research efforts with asking simulated humans via LLM roleplay, claims 90% accuracy. My presumption is this will work well on any given question, but that one must beware of too much optimization resulting in adversarial examples and thus very dumb mistakes. Identify authors. Fable 5.2 is dramatically underconfident in its identifications. When it has confidence of 25% or more it is right 87% of the time . Anthropic proves VP is not equal to VNP (which does not settle P vs. NP). Dramatically speed up your software development, writes Patrick McKenzie . Create a new Civilization-style game, Legatum , in your spare time using your personal AI subscriptions. Help make breakthroughs in physics . Create the United States as a Civilization-style hex map with lots of real data . Direct link here . Claude artifacts can now be turned into desktop apps . Epoch offers benchmark reviews . Some common ones have severe issues. Anthropic offers Siren, a test to see if agents can or will attempt to escape one of 26 sandboxes given various temptations, and what things make such escapes more likely. There is not a ton of talk about Gemini Neon, but what talk exists is quite good, including the minority that is not being directly amplified through Google employees. sysls : Let me say this in no uncertain terms. Gemini Neon has solved the hardest problems I could throw at it, clearing a bar no model, not even Fable 5.2, could. I’m not quite sure what happened here. Simon Sarris : There seems to be an enormous advantage that Gemini Neon simply thinks about problems differently. In a way its more strict with itself. If you made a codebase with Opus, ask Neon to critique it. You might be surprised what it turns up. Jeremy Howard : Yup, @GeminiApp Neon is actually as good as everyone is saying :D Dan Hendrycks (this contrasts with Kelsey Piper’s view on the actual writing): And it’s great at writing Jeremy Howard : So good. And also really good at teaching. Which makes it unique amongst current frontier models. Kelsey Piper : Gemini Carbon+Neon are currently unbeatable at “run this experiment and present me with some useful analysis of the results of it”. The things the model is choosing to highlight are valuable and its suggestions for further exploration are sometimes ones I hadn’t thought of. I keep trying to get the models to write prose well. It’s very hard. The specific thing I was interested in here is whether they can write Golden Age detective fiction – a genre they’ve invested a ton of – if I find an obscure book that’s not or barely is in their training data (when pushed they cannot reproduce any of its text), given the leadup to a scene, and are told to predict what comes next. (They’re better writers when asked to predict than when asked to write, because the latter cues them to do all their usual prancing prose-y nonsense.) Anyway I told Gemini basically the above, and it ran the experiment and then gave me some thoughts on the behavior of various different models as judges of how well the scene was written . I’m not claiming this is *itself well written*. But it was focused on the right features of its experiment and results – it knew which things to point out and its final note on the floor compression was useful. For the actual writing tasks Astra’s the runaway winner. Chan is correct, Google’s atomic naming system for models makes no sense at all. Calling the small model Hydrogen is an attempt to make it make sense, but it doesn’t, because they keep changing their logic every time. Agentic commerce is growing extremely quickly as the agents cross the line to where a normal consumer can find them net helpful. In the last three months we have seen an 80-fold increase. This is starting from a tiny base, so it is not impacting the overall economy yet. That will change. Is this a good agent or a bad agent? Mikhail Parakhin : I just saw Antigravity open a sidebar browser, go to Gemini website and start a Deep Research run there. I’m in a state of total disbelief: it is simultaneously super-cool and cringy-hacky. If you ever need help negotiating with your Kafkaian Agent Swarm that locks you out of your systems, Janus may be able to help . item.title: AI made self-hosting fun again
item.abstract:
I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit. I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me. Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that. Less friction Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project. Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort. In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me. Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality. Trying things I always found interesting There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them. NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server. For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time). Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week. AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations. Automating almost everything Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure. A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly. I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary. With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa. Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything. Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing. And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service. Back to more powerful hardware As I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server. For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though. I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place. It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site. Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life. Building my own tools But it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want. Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case. These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option. I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices , e-papers or Linux ISOs . I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs. They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem. What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running. The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to. Just because I can doesn’t mean I should Of course, there are downsides to all of this. Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes. There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place. On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point. And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to. A somewhat ironic development? I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life. I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency.

item.title: How to Future-Proof Your Data Career as Coding Agents Take Over Routine Work
item.abstract: How to Future-Proof Your Data Career as Coding Agents Take Over Routine Work The skills that keep you irreplaceable when AI handles the boilerplate. By Vinod Chugani on November 26, 2026 in Career Advice Something shifted quietly over the past year. The slog of data science (cleaning CSVs, writing boilerplate SQL, tuning hyperparameters) is now handled by AI. Coding agents have absorbed the grunt work that once defined entry-level data roles. If you spent two years perfecting your pandas wrangling or memorizing scikit-learn pipelines, you have good reason to pause and ask: what exactly is my value now? The honest answer is that your value hasn't disappeared. It's moved. The data scientist's role has shifted from model builder to system orchestrator. Autonomous agents and advanced large language models (LLMs) have automated most of the boilerplate coding, data cleaning, and basic statistical testing. The math of data science hasn't changed, but the interface has. That's both uncomfortable and liberating. Uncomfortable because the skills you built your early career on are depreciating faster than expected. Liberating because the skills that remain, the ones agents genuinely can't replicate, happen to be the most intellectually engaging parts of the work. What follows is a clear, honest strategy for staying indispensable as that transition accelerates. Understanding What Agents Actually Do (and Can't Do) Before you can future-proof your career, you need an accurate picture of what you're up against. AI coding agents can automate data science tasks like feature engineering and hyperparameter optimization. Think of an agent as a tool that significantly augments your work, automating manual tasks for a substantial productivity gain. That's the case in its favor. Here's where it breaks down. Coding agents excel at code but struggle with data science skepticism. They tend to celebrate early successes without flagging potential data quality issues, a gap that distinguishes pure coding assistance from actual data science. An agent will generate a model. It won't question whether the target variable was defined correctly, whether the training data reflects the population you care about, or whether the business actually needs a model at all. Despite everything LLMs and AI agents can do, a fundamental question remains: to what extent do human experts outperform autonomous AI agents on domain-specific data science tasks? In practice, the answer is quite a bit. In the most effective workflows, humans guide the problem-solving process while AI accelerates coding, experimentation, and iteration. The model can write the code. It can't own the decision. That distinction is about to define the entire future of data science, and it's your career strategy. Every section below is a direct response to something agents do poorly or can't do at all. Step 1: Become a Skilled Agent Orchestrator The most immediate shift you need to make is treating coding agents as colleagues you manage rather than tools you use. We're in a new era of building agents. The data scientist's role is being promoted from specialized coder to high-level strategic architect. In practice, that means learning how to structure problems in ways agents can execute reliably, how to verify their outputs, and when to override their suggestions. Here's what a well-designed agentic workflow actually looks like. You handle problem definition and meet with stakeholders to understand the business need. Specialized agents then work in parallel, handling data preparation, analysis, and initial modeling, logging their progress, flagging issues, and storing results. By automating the repetitive technical tasks, agents free you to focus on asking the right questions, finding new solutions, and driving real business impact. This isn't a passive upgrade. Learning to write precise, verifiable prompts for agents, design multi-step pipelines, and audit agent outputs critically is a genuine skill that takes time to develop. The practitioners who do it well will operate at dramatically higher leverage than those who don't. Resources for building this competency: DeepLearning.AI's "AI Agents in LangGraph" short course covers how to build and orchestrate agent pipelines, giving you the mental model you need to manage rather than just use these systems. Google's "Introduction to Responsible AI" on Coursera helps you understand what agents can and can't be trusted with, so you can design appropriate human checkpoints. Eric J. Ma's "How to Do Agentic Data Science" is a practitioner's ten lessons from actual experimentation with coding agents in real workflows. Step 2: Deepen Your Domain Expertise This is the step most technical practitioners underestimate, and the one that offers the most durable protection. Domain expertise ensures data science gets applied in the right context. Understanding industry-specific metrics, regulations, and processes is what allows you to generate insights that actually matter. Combining domain knowledge with technical skills ensures your models are relevant, interpretable, and aligned with actual business objectives. Agents have no industry context. They don't know that a churn model in telecommunications needs to account for seasonal contract renewals, that a fraud detection model in healthcare must comply with HIPAA constraints, or that the metric a marketing team has been optimizing for three years is a proxy for something else entirely. You can develop that understanding. Agents can't. The ability to help business leaders answer key questions, and even help them figure out which questions need answering in the first place, requires domain understanding that the model simply doesn't have. A professional with deep expertise in a specific vertical, whether that's fintech, clinical research, supply chain, or digital media, is genuinely difficult to replace. The agent has no way to acquire that contextual knowledge on its own. Resources for building domain depth: O'Reilly's industry-specific data science books cover domains from healthcare to finance to e-commerce with technical rigor. Industry newsletters and journals in your chosen vertical are underrated. Reading what practitioners care about, which metrics matter and which regulations are shifting, compounds into a real advantage over time. Coursera's industry specializations offer structured domain-focused credentials in areas like healthcare data science and financial technology. Step 3: Develop Statistical and Scientific Skepticism One of the clearest failure modes in an agent-augmented workflow: the agent produces output that looks correct. The numbers are plausible. The visualizations are clean. The model accuracy is respectable. And the entire thing is built on a flawed premise nobody caught. This is where statistical thinking becomes your most distinctive asset. Automation and AI handle repetitive tasks well, but they can't replace the critical thinking, domain knowledge, and creativity you bring. In a technical context, critical thinking means looking at a model's output and asking: does this make sense given what I know about causality here? Are there confounders? Is the evaluation metric aligned with the actual business outcome? Could this finding be a data artifact rather than a real signal? Agents pass through these questions without pausing. Experienced data scientists catch them. That gap in skepticism and scientific judgment is exactly what separates a dataset that produced a decision from a dataset that produced a costly mistake. Resources for strengthening statistical reasoning: StatQuest with Josh Starmer on YouTube remains one of the best resources for building genuine statistical intuition, not just procedural knowledge of when to apply which test. Calling Bullshit: The Art of Skepticism in a Data-Driven World by Carl Bergstrom and Jevin West trains exactly the kind of reasoning you need when evaluating agent outputs.

I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions.
